title: Your rehat
hookLine: whatever stage you're at, some rule of life can be yours

cards: Some listeners on this path wear a turban and have taken amrit. Some keep their hair and haven't. Some are learning the faith of a partner, a grandparent, a friend at school.
Some came because a line of Guru Nanak caught them and wouldn't let go. This block has read a code written with the initiated in mind, so it's fair to wonder where that leaves everyone else.
Today the code turns toward you, wherever you are. Not to sign anyone up; just to ask what a way of living looks like when it's small enough to start.

teach.h: ANG 305: A PORTRAIT OF A SIKH'S DAY.
teach.b: Guru Ram Das has a passage on Ang 305 that reads less like a rulebook and more like a portrait of a day.

In paraphrase: the one who calls themselves a Sikh of the true Guru rises early and remembers the Name, makes the effort to bathe in the pool of nectar, and keeps the Guru's word on their lips through the day.
Sitting or standing, they remember. And that Sikh, the passage says, is pleasing to the Guru. Look at how it's built.

teach.h: A SHAPE, NOT A LIST OF NOS.
teach.b: Not a list of prohibitions, but a shape: a morning, a day full of remembering, and love at the end of it. The full code sits on top of that shape and fills it in. Early on, your line was a way, not a list.
The word rehat means a way of living, how someone carries on day to day, and everyone has one. A person who checks their phone first thing has a rehat.
So does a person who skips breakfast and is short with people by noon. The question isn't whether to have one; it's whether to choose it. Nobody here is asked to take a vow.
But anyone can borrow the shape of that portrait: something for the morning, something to carry through the day, something to give.

teach.h: THREE SMALL RULES, CHOSEN ON PURPOSE.
teach.b: Three small rules, chosen on purpose, held for a while, and changed when they stop fitting. Some Sikh teachers describe the faith with three supports of their own: remember the Name, earn honestly, and share.

how: Some Sikh teachers point to the day Guru Ram Das describes on Ang 305 (rising early, remembering the Name, keeping the Guru's word through the day) as a model of daily practice, for the initiated and for those not yet initiated.

o: a vow every listener must take to join the Khalsa
the way you live each day, chosen on purpose
a written list of things you must never do

s: Guru Ram Das's portrait on Ang 305 is a list of prohibitions
it's a shape of a day: rise early, remember the Name, keep the Guru's word through the day.
everyone already has a rehat of some kind
a rehat is a way of living, day to day. the question is whether to choose it.

games.q: you've just written three rules. by the end of the week, one of them isn't working. what does today's lesson suggest?
o: change the one that doesn't fit, and keep going.
add five more to make up for it.
games.why: a beginner's rule of life is chosen on purpose, held for a while, and changed when it stops fitting.

practice: On paper or in your head, shape three short rules: one for the first few minutes of the morning, one to carry while you're out in the world, and one for giving, of time, attention or money. Make each small enough to keep tomorrow.
Then breathe with the three, and notice which one already feels like yours.

wordCard.voice: Your rehat. A rehat is a way of living, and everyone has one. Guru Ram Das paints a Sikh's day on Ang 305: rise early, remember, keep the word on your lips. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: a way of living, conduct; the root of rehat maryada, the Sikh code of conduct.

carryVoice: Your line: my three rules. Small enough to start, and real enough to keep. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ang 305 (Gauri ki Var, Guru Ram Das)
